title: He stole their hearts (2 Samuel 15:1–6)
hookLine: Absalom wins the people at the gate with flattery
carry: a kiss, a nod, a sigh

lines: YOUR MATTERS ARE GOOD AND RIGHT.
cards: Early morning at the gate of Jerusalem. A farmer has walked in from his town with a dispute, a boundary line, a debt, a stolen animal, to bring it to the king.
Before he reaches anyone official, a handsome young man steps out from beside the road. Where are you from? The farmer tells him.
The young man hears his case and nods. Your matters are good and right, he says. Then he lowers his voice.
But there's no one from the king to hear you.

teach.b: The young man is Absalom. Since Tamar, a lot has happened. He waited, had Amnon killed, and fled.
Years later he was allowed home, and his father kissed him. Now he gets a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run ahead of him, and goes to work at the gate. Look at his method.
He rises early and stands beside the road. He asks each person where they're from.

teach.h: YOUR CASE IS GOOD AND RIGHT.
teach.b: He tells every one of them their case is good and right, with only one side in front of him, and says the king has no one to listen.

teach.h: OH THAT I WERE MADE JUDGE.
teach.b: Then he sighs aloud: oh, that I were made judge in the land! Anyone with a cause could come to me, and I'd give them justice. When someone bows to him, he won't allow it; he takes hold of them and kisses them.
Every move is warm. Every move is aimed.
The text sums it up: "so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel."

teach.h: JACOB AND LABAN: THE SAME PHRASE.
teach.b: The same Hebrew phrase, to steal a heart, appears in Genesis when Jacob slips away from Laban without telling him, and there it means fooling him.
So the line has two edges: Absalom won their affection, and he did it by fooling them. He doesn't lie about everything. Maybe the courts really were slow.
Maybe people really did feel unheard. He takes a real grievance and makes himself the answer, and he never has to decide a single case. Saying yes to everyone is easy when you never have to rule.

how: Jews read Absalom at the gate as part of the book of Samuel, and later Jewish teaching uses a related phrase, genevat da'at, stealing the mind, for misleading someone.

o: a judge who hears cases at the gate
the heart, which Absalom quietly stole
a kiss of greeting at the city gate

games.q: he stole their hearts — tap the pairs.
p: your matters are good and right
oh that I were made judge

s: Absalom listened to both sides of each case
he told everyone who came with a suit that their case was good and right, with only their side in front of him.
the same phrase, steal the heart, is used of Jacob and Laban
in Genesis, Jacob slips away from Laban without telling him.
Absalom let people bow down to him
he took hold of them and kissed them instead.

games.q: you've walked to Jerusalem with a dispute. a handsome prince at the gate says your case is good and right, but the king won't hear you. what do you do?
o: thank him and wait for the king's judge anyway.
warm to him: at last, someone who gets it.
ask what the other side would say.
games.why: the text says Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel. his warmth worked, and the people turned toward him.

practice: Think back over the last few days to a moment when someone told you exactly what you wanted to hear, an ad, a voice online, a friend who agreed a little too fast, and ask the farmer's question: did they hear the other side?
Then turn it around, gently, to a moment when you said only what someone wanted to hear; no need to judge it, just see it clearly.

wordCard.voice: Lev. The Hebrew word for heart, the thing Absalom quietly stole from the men of Israel. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: heart. Absalom stole the lev, the heart, of the men of Israel.
